d: Love, benevolence, good will, esteem; plural: love-feasts.

e.t: This word means “love”: a committed concern and affection directed toward another person. In the Greek New Testament, it describes love shown toward God, toward fellow believers, and toward others. It can be expressed through patience, kindness, forgiveness, encouragement, and faithful care rather than mere feeling. The word occurs 116 times in the Greek New Testament, showing that love is a broad and recurring part of its message. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

d: Meal, flour.

e.t: This word means flour, the finely ground grain product used in baking. It is a concrete noun referring to an ordinary food ingredient rather than an abstract quality or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Matthew 13:33 and Luke 13:21. Both references belong to Jesus’ teaching about leaven being mixed into flour, but the word itself simply identifies the flour receiving the leaven. Its precise significance in either passage comes from the surrounding teaching, while its basic meaning remains straightforward: flour.

e.t: This word means “be an opponent” or “to be an opponent.” It describes someone or something that stands against another person, purpose, or work. Its focus is opposition rather than simple difference or distance. The word occurs eight times in the Greek New Testament, including passages that speak of opposition to Jesus’ work, to believers, or between opposing powers. The surrounding verse determines who is opposing whom and what is being resisted.

gl: to go away on a journey
d: To be away from home, go into another country, to be away, to be abroad.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular
Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This verb means “to go abroad” or “to go away on a journey.” It describes someone leaving one place to travel elsewhere, with attention to the departure or journey itself rather than a particular destination. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, appearing in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Its surrounding sentence determines whether the journey is simply travel or part of a larger situation, but the word itself consistently expresses going away on a journey.

e.t: This word means “carrying” or “to carry,” describing the action of bearing or taking something from one place or situation to another. It can refer to physically carrying an object, but its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 27 times across 27 verses, showing that it is a commonly used action word rather than a term limited to one setting. English translations commonly render it as “carry” or “carrying.”

d: A fuller, cloth-dresser, one who cleans woolen cloth.

e.t: This word refers to a bleacher—someone whose work is to bleach or whiten cloth. It is a noun describing a person by that occupation, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 9:3. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to a worker who treats cloth to make it clean or white.

d: To pass (of time); to continue through, intervene.

e.t: This word means “to pass” or “had passed.” It describes something moving beyond a point or an interval reaching its end, and it functions as an action word in a sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Mark and Acts. Its uses include references such as Mark 16:1, Acts 25:13, and Acts 27:9, but the surrounding verse is needed to show precisely what has passed in each case.

d: To cleanse thoroughly.
me: Verb, Future, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to clear out.” It is a Greek New Testament verb describing the act of removing what is present so that an area or collection is thoroughly emptied or cleaned. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew 3:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains straightforward: to clear away material completely rather than merely rearrange or inspect it.

d: A waking up, resurrection.

e.t: This word means “resurrection”: the rising of a dead person to life again. It names the event or reality of being raised from death, rather than merely describing ordinary waking or recovery. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 27:53. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains resurrection—the return from death to life. d: To persecute, expel by persecuting, drive out, vex, harass.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Participle, Genitive, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “to drive out” or “to persecute,” describing forceful opposition that seeks to remove or harass someone. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than a person, place, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Thessalonians 2:15. Its basic meaning remains focused on actively driving someone away or pursuing them with hostility; the surrounding verse determines which aspect is emphasized there.

d: Merciful, pitiful, miserable.

e.t: This word means “pitiful,” describing someone or something in a condition that calls for pity. It is an adjective, so it characterizes a person or situation rather than naming an action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Corinthians 15:19 and Revelation 3:17. Its basic sense remains focused on a miserable or pitiable condition; the surrounding verse determines exactly what situation is being described. It does not by itself explain the cause of that condition, but it identifies the condition as deserving compassion.

d: To lie in wait (ambush) for, seek to entrap (hence: to defraud, deceive).
me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Plural
Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to ambush” or “to wait in ambush”—to hide or position oneself secretly so an unsuspecting person can be seized or confronted. It describes deliberate, concealed waiting rather than an open meeting or direct approach. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Luke and Acts, and each occurrence belongs to a setting involving people watching for an opportunity to act. Its exact force in either verse is clarified by the surrounding passage.

e.t: This word means “to long for” or “to desire something deeply.” It describes an inward reaching toward something wanted, whether the object is a person, experience, or thing. In a sentence, it functions as a verb expressing strong desire rather than merely noticing or considering something. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek New Testament, so its precise force depends on what is being desired in each passage. Its central idea remains a powerful longing directed toward a particular object.

d: Opportune, timely, suitable; perhaps sometimes: holiday, festival.

e.t: This word means “opportune”: suitable or favorable for a particular purpose or moment. It describes something occurring at a fitting time, rather than simply something that happens at any time. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Mark 6:21 and Hebrews 4:16. Its exact force in either verse comes from the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains what is timely, fitting, or favorable.

d: Cleanness, purity.

e.t: This word means “cleanness,” describing a condition of being clean and free from impurity. It refers to the quality or state of cleanness rather than to an action of cleaning. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 9:13. Its precise force in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the condition of being clean or pure.

d: (literal: a level, ruler), a rule, regulation, rule of conduct or doctrine, (b) a measured (defined) area, province.

e.t: This word means “rule,” referring to a standard, boundary, or measure that determines the proper scope of something. It functions as a noun and is used four times in the Greek New Testament, all in 2 Corinthians and Galatians. In these passages, it describes the rule or measure by which work and conduct are assessed, rather than suggesting an unrestricted claim or reach. The exact force in any particular verse depends on its surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a governing standard or established boundary.

d: (a) empty, (b) empty (in moral content), vain, ineffective, foolish, worthless, (c) false, unreal, pretentious, hollow.

e.t: This word means “empty”: containing nothing, lacking what should be present, or being without the expected result. It is used in the Greek New Testament for something physically unfilled as well as for a condition or effort that proves fruitless. The word occurs 18 times in 16 New Testament verses, so its basic sense is consistent while its precise application depends on the surrounding sentence. It can describe an empty container, an unproductive situation, or work that would otherwise have no meaningful outcome.

d: (literal: partnership) (a) contributory help, participation, (b) sharing in, communion, (c) spiritual fellowship, a fellowship in the spirit.

e.t: This word means “fellowship” and “participation”—sharing in something together rather than remaining separate. In the New Testament, it describes a common bond, shared involvement, or partnership among people, and may also describe participation connected with Christ. It occurs 19 times in 17 verses in the Greek New Testament, with “fellowship” as its recognized English rendering. Its normal sense centers on belonging together and taking part together.

d: (a) to reveal, make known (in a law court), to lay information, inform, (b) to make known, point out.

e.t: This word means “to disclose” or “to inform”—making something known to another person. It describes the act of communicating information that was not previously known, whether by reporting it or bringing it to someone’s attention. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, showing a focused use connected with passing on information. The surrounding passage determines exactly what is disclosed and why, but the central idea remains making information known.

d: Ten thousand; also used for a very large number, innumerable.

e.t: This word describes an extremely large number—“innumerable” or a “myriad.” It points to a quantity so vast that ordinary counting is not the focus. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, showing that it can describe a very great amount in different sentences. Its central idea remains the same: an exceptionally large, practically countless number rather than a small or precisely emphasized quantity.

e.t: This word means “being understood” or “to understand.” It describes grasping the meaning of something so that it becomes clear to the mind. In the Greek New Testament, it is used 14 times, including passages where Jesus’ hearers are expected to comprehend his teaching or recognize the significance of what he says. Its central idea is therefore mental understanding: perceiving meaning rather than merely hearing words. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: With one mind, unanimously, with one accord, at the same time.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “united,” describing people acting together rather than separately. It expresses a shared unity and common purpose among those involved. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 11 times, beginning in Acts and appearing once in Romans. Its use in these writings consistently presents togetherness as the central idea, while the surrounding verse determines the specific activity or situation in which people are united.

d: (a) a male child, boy, (b) a male slave, servant; thus: a servant of God, especially as a title of the Messiah, (c) a female child, girl.

e.t: This word refers to a child or boy. It is a general term for a young person, and its exact reference—whether to a child in a household, a servant, or another young person—comes from the surrounding sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 24 times, appearing in Matthew, Luke, John, and Acts. The central idea remains a young person described as a child or boy, rather than an abstract quality or action.

d: To dwell around, to be neighboring to.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Accusative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word describes living around other people or dwelling in a neighborhood. It refers to residence among nearby inhabitants, emphasizing a person’s place within a surrounding community rather than simply being present somewhere. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Luke 1:65. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning is residence among those living in the same area.

d: (a) a maker, poet, (b) a doer, carrier out, performer.

e.t: This word means a “doer”—a person who carries something out through action rather than merely hearing, knowing, or speaking about it. It describes someone who puts words or commands into practice. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, including repeated use in James for the person who acts on what is heard. Its basic focus is active obedience or performance, depending on what is being done in the surrounding sentence.

d: Very hungry.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “hungry,” and it can also express being “very hungry.” It describes a strong physical need for food, with the second gloss highlighting greater intensity. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Acts 10:10. Its basic meaning remains focused on hunger itself, while the surrounding verse determines how that condition functions in the passage.

e.t: This word means “Samaritan,” identifying a person as a Samaritan. It is a designation tied to the people called Samaritans in the Greek New Testament. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both occurrences appearing in John 4:9. Its lexical meaning is straightforward, while the surrounding passage determines what is being said about the Samaritan in that verse. Here, it functions as a personal group designation rather than a general description.

d: Susannah, a woman of the retinue of Jesus.

e.t: Susanna is a personal name, referring to a woman rather than expressing an action, quality, or teaching. In the Greek New Testament, it identifies one woman named in Luke 8:3. The name is preserved as “Susanna” in the English translations represented here. Because it is a proper name, its basic meaning is identification: it tells the reader who a person is, while the surrounding verse supplies her particular role and circumstances.

d: To strengthen, confirm, establish, settle.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular
Verb, Aorist, Passive, Indicative, third, Plural
Verb, Imperfect, Passive, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to make strong” or “to strengthen.” It describes the giving or receiving of strength, whether referring to a person becoming physically strong or believers being strengthened in their faith and life together. The word occurs three times in the New Testament Greek corpus, all in Acts, showing a focused use rather than a broad range of unrelated meanings. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: A joint imitator.

e.t: This word describes a fellow imitator—someone who imitates along with another person or group. It presents imitation as a shared activity rather than something done alone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so its precise force in Philippians 3:17 depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains clear: joining others in following the same example or pattern.

d: A bow.

e.t: The word means “bow,” referring to the weapon used to shoot arrows. It is a noun naming an object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Revelation 6:2. The available wording consistently renders it as “bow,” supporting this straightforward sense. Its exact significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which should be read separately.

d: Food, nourishment, maintenance.

e.t: This word means “food,” referring to what people eat for bodily nourishment. It is a noun used for ordinary physical provision, whether discussing what someone consumes, what a household needs, or what is supplied to others. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 16 times across 16 verses, consistently pointing to food as a basic human need rather than to an abstract idea. Its precise significance in any verse comes from the surrounding passage.

d: (a) to remain behind, (b) to stand my ground, show endurance, (c) to endure, bear up against, persevere.

e.t: This word means to endure, remain, or stay behind rather than give up or leave. It describes continuing through difficulty or remaining in place when others move on. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 17 times, so its use includes both perseverance and the simpler idea of staying behind. The surrounding sentence determines which aspect is most prominent, but the central thought is continuing to remain under circumstances that might lead someone to depart.

d: Poverty, want, need.

e.t: This word refers to need or poverty—the condition of lacking what is necessary or having very little. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, so it is a relatively uncommon word rather than a broad term repeated throughout many passages. Its meaning can describe material lack, while the surrounding verse determines how that lack is being presented. It is used once in Mark and once in Philippians, with “poverty” representing its sense in Mark.

d: Phlegon, a Roman Christian man.

e.t: Phlegon is a personal name identifying an individual mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It does not function as a general description or action word; it distinguishes this person from others named in the passage. The name occurs once, in Romans 16:14, and is rendered as “Phlegon.” The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the person’s specific role in that passage.

d: Chalcedony, a small stone of various colors.

e.t: This word means “chalcedony,” the name of a particular stone. It functions as a noun identifying the stone itself rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 21:19. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, this cached meaning identifies the stone named by the word without adding details about its symbolic role or appearance in that passage.

d: Grass, herbage, growing grain, hay.

e.t: This word means grass—the green vegetation that grows from the ground. In the Greek New Testament, it is a noun used for ordinary grass, whether described as covering a field, being cut for people to sit on, or appearing among other plants. It occurs 15 times in 13 verses, showing that the word is used across several kinds of passages while keeping the same basic meaning. Its precise significance in any one verse comes from the surrounding context, but the word itself refers simply to grass.
